s001.text: UPSC, twenty nineteen. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Can Parliament destroy the Constitution's basic structure by expanding its own amending power? Here's the strange part. Parliament once wrote a clause that tried to do exactly that.

s002.text: Read what it asks. Explain whether means give a reasoned yes or no. And there are four jobs. Explain the statement. Show what Article three sixty-eight allows. Answer whether the power can grow. Then weigh it.

s003.text: Start with the power itself. Article three sixty-eight lets Parliament add, change or repeal any provision. It needs a special majority in each House. Some changes also need half the States.

s004.text: But in nineteen seventy-three, thirteen judges sat in Kesavananda Bharati. By seven to six, they set a limit. The power to amend does not include the power to alter the basic structure.

s005.text: So in nineteen seventy-six, Parliament pushed back. The Forty-second Amendment added two clauses. One said no court could question any amendment. The other said there was no limit whatever on the power.

s006.text: But in nineteen eighty, in Minerva Mills, all five judges struck both clauses down. Their reason is the line in our question. A limited power cannot enlarge itself into an absolute one. The power to destroy is not a power to amend.

s007.text: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open by naming where the statement comes from. That one line shows you know the case.

s008.text: Section one is the power. Three short points: what it allows, the special majority, and Article thirteen kept out.

s009.text: Section two answers the question directly: no. Then prove it in order. Kesavananda sets the limit. The Forty-second Amendment tries to remove it. Minerva Mills strikes that down. And it still applies: in twenty fifteen, the judicial appointments amendment fell four to one.

s010.text: Section three weighs it. Parliament can still amend any part, within the limit. The courts decide where the limit is. And Ambedkar's point keeps change open. Win two-thirds, and you can change the text, inside the limit.

s011.text: Now the easy answer beside it. It says the basic structure is written in the Constitution. It isn't. It says Kesavananda gave a fixed list. Even NCERT says that is debated. It repeats a common myth about Indira Gandhi's case. It says Fundamental Rights can never be amended. And it never mentions the two clauses the question is about.

s012.text: Here is the payoff. One timeline answers its cousins. Twenty sixteen asked about the Coelho case. The PSIR paper asked about Article three sixty-eight and parliamentary sovereignty. Learn the timeline once. The full story of the case gets its own episode in our Polity series.
